title: The Orange That Turns Green: Potassium Dichromate
subject: Chemistry
objective: Potassium dichromate is made from chromite ore: fusion with sodium carbonate in air gives yellow sodium chromate (Fe₂O₃ is filtered off), acid turns it into orange sodium dichromate (two CrO₄ tetrahedra share one oxygen), and KCl precipitates the less soluble K₂Cr₂O₇. Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH while Cr stays +6. In acid, Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (E° = 1.33 V): a strong oxidising agent that turns orange to green, oxidising Fe²⁺, I⁻, H₂S and, in the 1954 breathalyser, ethanol.

short.q: Describe the preparation of potassium dichromate from chromite ore with equations.
short.solution: 4FeCr₂O₄ + 8Na₂CO₃ + 7O₂ → 8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ + 8CO₂; filter off Fe₂O₃; 2Na₂CrO₄ + 2H⁺ → Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2Na⁺ + H₂O; Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl (orange crystals).

short.q: Explain the effect of pH on a dichromate solution.
short.solution: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O. Acid favours orange dichromate; base (OH⁻) converts it back to yellow chromate. Cr remains +6, so the change is not redox.

right: orange, two tetrahedra sharing one O
